items.stem: Suppose you made up your own ‘atom’, as Thomson described, using clay for the positive charge and small beads for the electrons spread through it. What will happen if: (i) the positive charge on the clay is lesser than the total negative charge of the beads? (ii) by mistake, the clay itself carries a bit of negative charge? Would your model still represent a neutral atom?
items.answer: (i) If the positive charge on the clay is less than the total negative charge of the beads, the overall atom would become a negatively charged ion. This contradicts the fundamental observation that atoms in their normal state are electrically neutral. (ii) Your model would no longer represent a neutral atom because the clay is supposed to be the sole source of balancing positive charge. If the clay carries a negative charge, the entire structure becomes overwhelmingly negative and cannot balance the negative charge of the beads.

items.stem: Could an orange or a lemon, which also contain seeds inside soft pulp, be a good comparison? In what ways does it match Thomson’s idea and where does it fall short?
items.answer: An orange or lemon can be a reasonable comparison because the discrete seeds embedded within the soft pulp nicely represent the negatively charged electrons scattered within a larger positive mass. However, it falls short because Thomson’s model describes the positive charge as a uniform, continuous sphere, whereas a citrus fruit has broken segments, empty spaces, and a thick outer rind that do not represent a uniform positive field.

items.stem: Why did Thomson conclude that electrons are present in all atoms?
items.answer: Thomson found that the nature of the cathode rays, which consist of electrons, was completely independent of the material of the cathode or the gas used inside the vacuum tube. Because every different element he tested emitted the exact same negatively charged, lightweight particles, he logically concluded that electrons must be a fundamental subatomic component present in all atoms.

items.stem: What do you think would happen if alpha- particles were replaced with negatively charged particles in Rutherford’s gold foil experiment?
items.answer: If negatively charged particles were used, they would be attracted to the densely packed, positively charged nucleus instead of being repelled by it. As a result, many particles might be deflected inward towards the nucleus or captured entirely, meaning we would not observe the sharp backward scattering that occurs due to electrostatic repulsion.

items.stem: Rutherford found that a few alpha-particles bounced back sharply. How does this single surprising result completely rule out Thomson’s ‘plum pudding model’ of the atom?
items.answer: In Thomson’s model, the positive charge and mass are spread thinly and evenly throughout the entire atom, meaning an energetic, heavy alpha particle should easily punch straight through with at most a slight deflection. The fact that a few alpha particles bounced backward meant they must have collided with something incredibly dense and highly positively charged. This single observation proved that the positive mass is not spread uniformly, but is instead concentrated into a tiny, massive central nucleus.

items.stem: If you could ask Rutherford one question about his work, what would it be?
items.answer: I would ask him what his initial reaction was at the exact moment his assistants reported that some alpha particles had actually bounced backward. I would love to know if he immediately realized the plum pudding model was wrong or if he first suspected an error in the experiment.

items.stem: A logistics company is loading heavy cargo crates, each weighing 1000 N, into a delivery truck. The flat bed of the truck is exactly 1.5 metres above the ground level. The workers initially attempt to lift the crates vertically but find it physically exhausting. They decide to use a sturdy wooden plank as a sliding ramp. First, they try a 3-metre- long ramp, which requires a moderate push. Later, they switch to a longer 5-metre plank. The workers immediately notice a significant difference in how hard they have to push to move the same crates up into the truck. QUESTIONS: (a) What type of simple machine is the wooden ramp used by the workers? (b) Calculate the theoretical mechanical advantage of the 3-metre-long ramp. (c) How does using the ramp make the work easier for the workers compared to lifting the crates vertically? Mention the physical trade- off involved. (d) Explain why the 5-metre-long ramp made it easier to push the crates compared to the 3-metre-long ramp.
items.answer: (a) The wooden ramp is an inclined plane. (b) Mechanical advantage of an inclined plane = Length of the plane (L) / Height (h) = 3 m / 1.5 m = 2. (c) The ramp makes work easier by allowing the workers to apply a smaller force over a longer distance to raise the crate to the same height. The trade-off is that while the effort required is smaller, the distance over which the effort must be applied increases, keeping total work done constant. (d) The 5-metre ramp is longer, meaning it has a gentler slope. Since mechanical advantage equals Length/Height, increasing the length for the same height increases the mechanical advantage. Therefore, less effort force is required to move the load up the longer ramp.

The seesaw consists of a long, rigid board resting on a fixed central pivot point. Aryan, who is heavier with a mass of 40 kg, sits 1.5 metres away from the pivot on the left side. Initially, the seesaw heavily drops down on Aryan’s Choose the correct option: (i) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. (ii) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. (iii) A is true, but R is false. (iv) A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: The correct option is (ii) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. Assertion A is true Rutherford’s gold foil experiment proved mass is concentrated in the nucleus. Reason R is also true Thomson proposed electrons embedded in uniform positive charge. However, R doesn’t explain A; Rutherford’s conclusion actually disproved Thomson’s model.

items.stem: Imagine you are a scientist who has discovered a new element. Name this element after yourself and justify that the symbol you have chosen follows the IUPAC rules.
items.answer: If I discovered a new element and named it “Nivium” after myself, I would assign it the symbol “Nv”. This choice perfectly follows IUPAC rules because the first letter “N” is capitalized and the second letter “v” is lowercase. Additionally, it uses the first letter along with another prominent letter from the name, ensuring it does not conflict with existing symbols like “N” for Nitrogen or “Ni” for Nickel.

items.stem: What problems could arise if every scientist used different symbols for the same element?
items.answer: If every scientist used different symbols, it would create massive confusion and communication breakdowns within the global scientific community. Standardized symbols bypass language barriers, so without them, sharing research, writing chemical formulas, and collaborating on international projects would become incredibly tedious and prone to dangerous errors.

items.stem: An atom with an atomic number of 26 has 56 nucleons. Find out its number of electrons, protons and neutrons.
items.answer: The atomic number is 26, so the atom has 26 protons, and since it is a neutral atom, it also has 26 electrons. The number of neutrons is found by subtracting the atomic number from the total number of nucleons (mass number), which is 56 minus 26, resulting in 30 neutrons.

items.stem: The nucleus of an atom contains 20 protons. If its mass number is 41, find the number of neutrons in it.
items.answer: The number of neutrons is calculated by subtracting the number of protons from the mass number. Therefore, 41 minus 20 gives 21 neutrons.

items.stem: An atom has 18 neutrons and an atomic number of 17. What is its mass number?
items.answer: The mass number is the sum of the protons (which is equal to the atomic number) and the neutrons. Adding 17 protons and 18 neutrons gives a mass number of 35.

items.stem: An atom 23A has 11 electrons. Find the number of neutrons in it.
items.answer: The notation indicates that the mass number is 23 and the atomic number is 11, meaning it has 11 protons. To find the neutrons, subtract the atomic number from the mass number, which is 23 minus 11, giving 12 neutrons.

items.stem: Identify the number of electrons in the outermost shell of the following elements: (i) C12 6 (ii) F 9 19 (iii) Si 14 28
items.answer: (i) Carbon (atomic number 6) has an electronic configuration of 2, 4, so it has 4 electrons in its outermost shell. (ii) Fluorine (atomic number 9) has an electronic configuration of 2, 7, so it has 7 electrons in its outermost shell. (iii) Silicon (atomic number 14) has an electronic configuration of 2, 8, 4, so it has 4 electrons in its outermost shell.

items.stem: Interpret the atomic structure shown in the diagram. Which of the following options correctly identifies the atomic number, mass number, and valency of this atom respectively?
items.answer: The atomic number equals the total number of protons (6). The mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons (6 + 8 = 14). With 6 electrons configured as 2, 4, the outermost valence shell contains 4 electrons. To complete its octet, the atom requires 4 more electrons, resulting in a valency of 4.

items.stem: What specifically is an alpha particle, which Ernest Rutherford uniquely utilized during his famous gold foil scattering experiment?
items.answer: During the famous gold foil experiment conducted by Geiger and Marsden strictly under Rutherford’s direct guidance, the powerful energetic beam consisted primarily of alpha particles. An alpha particle is structurally identical to the nucleus of a fundamental helium atom, inherently consisting of exactly two firmly bound protons and exactly two stabilizing internal nuclear neutral neutrons.

items.stem: The composition of the nuclei of three atomic species X, Y, and Z are given as follows. Species Number of Protons Number of Neutrons Species X 18 19 Species Y 17 18 Species Z 17 20 Explain the relation between the following: (i) Y and Z (ii) Z and X
items.answer: (i) Species Y and Z are isotopes. They both have the same number of protons (atomic number 17) but different numbers of neutrons (18 and 20, respectively), meaning they are atoms of the same element with different mass numbers. (ii) Species Z and X are isobars. The mass number of Z is 37 (17 protons + 20 neutrons) and the mass number of X is also 37 (18 protons + 19 neutrons). They are atoms of different elements (different proton numbers) that have the exact same mass number.

items.stem: What conclusion did Rutherford draw about the position and characteristics of the atom’s positively charged part based on the few alpha particles that bounced back or were deflected at large angles in the gold foil experiment?
items.answer: Rutherford concluded that the positively charged part of the atom is not spread uniformly throughout the atom, but is heavily concentrated in an extremely small, dense region at the very center, which he named the nucleus. He deduced this because only a massive, concentrated positive charge could exert enough repulsive force to cause the heavy, fast-moving, positively charged alpha particles to deflect sharply or bounce straight back.

items.stem: Explain and arrange the following statements in the correct chronological order to show how atomic models have evolved over time. (i) Bohr’s model proposed that electrons move in fixed orbits around the nucleus, each with a definite energy. (ii) Thomson’s model depicted the atom as a ‘plum pudding’ with electrons embedded in a sphere of positive charge. (iii) Rutherford’s model proposed that atoms have a dense central nucleus. (iv) Dalton’s model described atoms as indivisible particles.
items.answer: The correct chronological order is (iv), (ii), (iii), (i). First, Dalton proposed his theory that matter is composed of solid, indivisible particles called atoms. Decades later, Thomson discovered the electron and modified this view with his plum pudding model, suggesting the atom was a positively charged sphere containing embedded negative electrons. Later, Rutherford conducted his gold foil experiment, which disproved Thomson’s model by revealing that the positive charge is concentrated in a tiny, dense central nucleus. Finally, Bohr refined Rutherford’s nuclear model by introducing the concept of stationary orbits to explain why orbiting electrons do not lose energy and collapse into the nucleus. Journey Inside the Atom

items.stem: Electrons move around the nucleus in orbits. Why do they not fly away from the atom? Explain what keeps them attracted to the nucleus.
items.answer: Electrons do not fly away from the atom because they carry a negative electrical charge, while the nucleus contains protons which carry a positive electrical charge. This creates a strong electrostatic force of attraction between the nucleus and the electrons. This attractive force pulls the electrons toward the center, acting as the centripetal force required to keep them moving in their circular orbits around the nucleus.

items.stem: Assertion (A): The discovery of subatomic particles helped in understanding the atomic structure. Reason (R): The number of electrons is equal to the number of protons in an atom. Choose the correct option: (i) Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A. (ii) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. (iii) A is true, but R is false. (iv) A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: The correct option is (ii) Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. It is true that discovering electrons, protons, and neutrons revealed that atoms have internal structure, proving Dalton’s indivisible theory wrong (Assertion A is true). It is also true that in a neutral atom, protons equal electrons (Reason R is true). However, this mathematical equality is not the fundamental reason why the discovery of subatomic particles helped us understand the physical structure and arrangement of the atom.

items.answer: (i) 12 protons (The number of protons is equal to the atomic number). (ii) 12 neutrons (Calculated by subtracting the atomic number from the mass number: 24 - 12 = 12). (iii) 12 electrons (In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons).

items.stem: Both Rutherford’s and Bohr’s models have electrons orbiting the nucleus. Why did Rutherford’s model fail to explain atomic stability, while Bohr’s model succeeded?
items.answer: Rutherford’s model failed because it proposed electrons orbiting randomly like planets. According to the laws of physics, a charged particle moving in a circular path accelerates and must continuously radiate energy. Therefore, Rutherford’s orbiting electron would lose energy, spiral inward, and collapse into the nucleus. Bohr’s model succeeded by introducing the postulate that electrons revolve only in specific, allowed circular paths called stationary states or discrete shells. He established that while moving in these fixed energy levels, electrons do not emit energy, thereby perfectly explaining why the atom remains stable.

items.stem: An atom 70 X has 31 electrons. How many neutrons are there in its nucleus?
items.answer: In a neutral atom, the number of protons equals the number of electrons, so this atom has 31 protons. The mass number is given as 70. The number of neutrons is found by subtracting the number of protons from the mass number (70 - 31), which means there are 39 neutrons in its nucleus.

items.stem: An atom has 79 protons and a mass number of 197. Calculate (i) the number of neutrons, and (ii) the number of electrons. (i) the number of neutrons (ii) the number of electrons
items.answer: (i) The number of neutrons is 118. This is calculated by subtracting the number of protons from the mass number (197 - 79 = 118). (ii) The number of electrons is 79. Assuming the atom is electrically neutral, it must have the exact same number of negative electrons as it has positive protons.

items.stem: Aman was discussing the structure of atom with his classmates. During the discussion, he learnt that an element X has a mass number of 35 and contains 18 neutrons. Based on this information, answer the following questions: (i) How many electrons and protons does element X have? (ii) What is its atomic number? (iii) Identify the element X. (iv) Write its electronic configuration. (v) How many valence electrons does it have? (vi) What will be the mass number if two neutrons are added to its nucleus? (vii)What will be the relation of X with the new atom? Journey Inside the Atom
items.answer: (i) Element X has 17 protons (Mass number 35 - 18 neutrons = 17) and 17 electrons, as the number of electrons equals the number of protons in a neutral atom. (ii) The atomic number is 17, which is equal to the number of protons. (iii) Element X is Chlorine (Cl), as chlorine has an atomic number of 17. (iv) The electronic configuration of Chlorine (17 electrons) is 2, 8, 7. (v) It has 7 valence electrons, which are the electrons present in its outermost shell. (vi) The new mass number will be 37 (Original mass 35 + 2 additional neutrons). (vii)Element X (mass 35) and the new atom (mass 37) will be isotopes, because they have the same atomic number (17) but different mass numbers due to a different number of neutrons.

items.stem: In an atom, there are 12 protons and 12 neutrons in the nucleus. Now, imagine that all the electrons are replaced with some hypothetical particles that have the same charge as electrons but are 500 times heavier. What effect will this replacement have on the atom’s: (i) Atomic number (ii) Atomic mass (iii) Mass number (iv) Overall charge
items.answer: (i) The atomic number will remain unchanged (12). The atomic number is strictly determined by the number of protons in the nucleus, which has not been altered. (ii) The atomic mass will increase. Normally, the mass of electrons is negligible compared to the nucleus. Replacing them with particles 500 times heavier adds significant, non-negligible mass to the entire atom. (iii) The mass number will remain unchanged (24). Mass number is defined solely as the total number of nucleons (protons + neutrons) inside the nucleus, which remains 12 + 12. (iv) The overall charge will remain unchanged (neutral). The hypothetical particles possess the exact same negative electrical charge as normal electrons, so 12 of them will still perfectly balance the positive charge of the 12 protons in the nucleus.
